extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, literary criticism, and Coleridge's works
extracted.subtask_description: Expository/philosophical prose analyzing the nature of association, memory, perception, and the conditions for philosophy as a science; aimed at developing conceptual standards for acceptable theories of mind and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of association — vividness determines recall
rubrics_metrics.description: The true practical general law of association: that whatever makes certain parts of a total impression more vivid or distinct than the rest, will determine the mind to recall these in preference to others equally linked together by the common condition of contemporaneity (or contiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: seeing a mackerel may immediately evoke gooseberries because they were eaten together; vivid or distinct parts of an impression are preferentially recalled. Use vividness and distinctness as explanatory factors when evaluating why particular associations arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active will and attention can intensify memory (vs. artificial mnemonics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The will itself, by confining and intensifying the attention, may arbitrarily give vividness or distinctness to any object whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this follows a critique of 'recent schemes' promising artificial memory: such schemes are useless or absurd and can produce confusion and a debasement of the fancy. Emphasize disciplined attention rather than mechanical mnemonic tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of Memory — physiological and moral conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound logic; philosophical knowledge of facts under the relation of cause and effect; a cheerful and communicative temper; a quiet conscience; a condition free from anxieties; sound health; and above all (as far as relates to passive remembrance) a healthy digestion — these are the best, these are the only Arts of Memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing memory or recommending practices to improve passive remembrance, prioritize intellectual habits (logic, knowledge), temperament (cheerful, communicative), moral state (quiet conscience), and physical well-being (health, digestion) over artificial techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑existence requirement for association
rubrics_metrics.description: All association demands and presupposes the existence of the thoughts and images to be associated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Association cannot create its elements ex nihilo; any account of association must accept that the items to be associated already exist in some form in the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual theory must include co‑adequate mechanism in the percipient
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis that an external world exactly correspondent to images (or modifications of our being) exists does not explain perception; it neither involves the explanation nor precludes the necessity of a mechanism and co-adequate forces in the percipient, which at the impulse from without are to create anew the correspondent object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere pre-existence of an 'original' does not solve formation of a copy: a viable theory of perception must posit internal processes or capacities in the percipient that can produce the perceptual object, not rely solely on external correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate presence of the object in perception (not a logical product)
rubrics_metrics.description: In our immediate perception, it is not the mere power or act of the object, but the object itself, which is immediately present. It is the object itself, not the product of a 'logism,' which is present to our consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that reduce perception to chains of deduction or mere effects; acceptable accounts should account for the felt immediacy of objects in consciousness rather than treating perception as inferentially constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific explanatory parsimony — limit attributes and avoid occult multiplication (critique of Hylozoism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis of Hylozoism is the death of all rational physiology and of all physical science; physical science requires a limitation of terms and cannot consist with the arbitrary power of multiplying attributes by occult qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scientific and philosophical hypotheses by their restraint in ontological commitments and avoidance of ad hoc multiplication of properties. Theories that unduly multiply occult qualities are judged to undermine rational explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality requires homogeneity of relata
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causality holds only between homogeneous things, that is, things having some common property; and cannot extend from one world into another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking causal explanation between domains (e.g., mind and matter), require some shared or compatible properties; treat cross‑ontological causation as problematic unless homogeneity can be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory adequacy as a test of materialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism has hitherto left incomprehensible how any affection from without can metamorphose itself into perception or will; to explain thinking as a material phenomenon one must reduce matter to a modification of intelligence, and if made intelligible materialism ceases to be materialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge materialist accounts by whether they genuinely show how external impacts become inner awareness; if the account requires reducing matter to mental aspects, it loses its materialist character — a sign of theoretical failure or category collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary postulate for philosophy as science — co‑inherence of intelligence and being
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy (as the affectionate seeking after truth) requires assuming as a postulate that Truth is correlative of Being; that intelligence and being are ab initio identical and co-inherent; intelligence and being are reciprocally each other's substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a condition for treating philosophy as a systematic science rather than mere classification, one may need to posit a fundamental unity between mind (intelligence) and being; evaluate philosophical systems on whether they can coherently adopt or reject this postulate and the consequences thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in teaching philosophy; distinguish letter and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: A vindication of prudence in the teaching of Philosophy — the difference between the letter and the spirit (of Kant's writings) is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting philosophical doctrine, teachers and writers should be prudent: distinguish literal formulations ('letter') from the intended underlying principles ('spirit'), and avoid misleading literalism in pedagogical exposition.
